w: A limestone hill jutting 277 metres above central Athens, its summit the highest point in the city and reachable by funicular from a station tucked into Kolonaki. Pine trees cover the slopes below a 19th-century chapel, a theatre and a restaurant sharing the same sweeping view.
s: Athens's highest point, reached by funicular
_facts: Cretaceous limestone hill, 277 metres above sea level, highest point in central Athens
Ascended by the Lycabettus Funicular from Aristippou Street in Kolonaki
Two peaks hold the 19th-century Chapel of St. George, a theatre, and a restaurant

w: Built specifically to house everything ever pulled from the Acropolis rock and its slopes - Bronze Age to Byzantine - and it sits directly over excavated ruins of Roman and early Byzantine Athens. More than 4,250 objects fill 14,000 square metres, opened only in 2009 after decades of debate.
s: A museum built literally over ancient Athens
_facts: Archaeological museum for findings from the Acropolis site, founded 2003, opened to public 20 June 2009
Lies over ruins of part of Roman and early Byzantine Athens
More than 4,250 objects exhibited over 14,000 square metres

w: The best-preserved ancient Greek temple anywhere, still largely intact after two and a half thousand years - and the reason is almost an accident. From the 7th century until 1834 it served as a Greek Orthodox church, which likely saved this Doric masterpiece from the ruin that swallowed its neighbours.
s: The best-preserved temple in Greece - by accident
_facts: Well-preserved Doric peripteral Greek temple dedicated to Hephaestus, on Agoraios Kolonos hill at the Agora of Athens
From the 7th century until 1834 served as the Greek Orthodox church of Saint George Akamates
Remains standing largely intact today

w: An octagonal marble tower from around 50 BC that functioned as sundial, water clock and weather vane all at once, its eight reliefs of wind gods still ringing the top. It is the only horologium to survive intact from classical antiquity - a clock tower nobody ever quite stopped using.
_facts: Octagonal Pentelic marble tower in the Roman Agora, named for eight reliefs of wind gods
Completed by about 50 BC at the latest
Only surviving horologium (clock tower) from classical antiquity, continuously occupied for different functions
Housed a large water clock and incorporated sundials

w: The commercial and civic heart of ancient Athens, spread beneath the Acropolis between the Areopagus and the Agoraios Kolonos hill - the marketplace, meeting ground and residential quarter where Athenian public life actually happened, day to day, for centuries.
s: Where ancient Athenian life actually happened
_facts: Ancient Greek agora, also called the Classical Agora, northwest of the Acropolis
Bounded south by the Areopagus hill, west by the Agoraios Kolonos (Market Hill)
Initial use was commercial, assembly, and residential gathering place

w: The birthplace of theatre itself, cut into the Acropolis's south slope from the mid-6th century BC as part of the sanctuary of Dionysus the Liberator. By the 4th century BC it held up to 25,000 people for the City Dionysia, before sinking into Byzantine decay.
s: Where Western theatre itself was invented
_facts: Ancient Greek theatre on the south slope of the Acropolis, part of the sanctuary of Dionysus Eleuthereus
First orchestra terrace built around the mid- to late-6th century BC, hosted the City Dionysia
Reached fullest extent in the 4th century BC, capacity up to 25,000, used through the Roman period
Fell into decay in the Byzantine era, excavated and restored in the 19th century

w: Named for the constitution wrung out of King Otto after an 1843 uprising - the square still sits in front of the Old Royal Palace, now home to the Greek Parliament, making it the literal front lawn of modern Greek politics.
s: Named for a constitution won by uprising in 1843
_facts: Central square of Athens, named after the Constitution King Otto was obliged to grant
Followed a popular and military uprising on 3 September 1843
Located in front of the 19th-century Old Royal Palace, home of the Greek Parliament since 1934
Most important square of modern Athens historically and socially

w: A Roman-era stone theatre finished in AD 161 on the Acropolis's southwest slope, renovated in 1950 and still hosting performances beneath the same ancient tiers. Turn up at dusk during the Athens Festival and you're watching a stage that's drawn crowds for two thousand years.
s: A Roman theatre still staging shows since AD 161
_facts: Stone Greek theatre structure on the southwest slope of the Acropolis
Completed AD 161, renovated in 1950

w: A monumental complex Emperor Hadrian raised in AD 132, its reading rooms once lined with papyrus scrolls behind a grand Corinthian entrance of Karystian marble. Sacked in the Herulian invasion of 267, it was later colonised by three successive Byzantine churches, one Athens's first cathedral.
s: A Roman emperor's library, later three churches
_facts: Ruin of a monumental building created by Emperor Hadrian in AD 132, north side of the Acropolis
Reading rooms held papyrus scrolls; entrance via the Stoa of Hadrian with Karystian marble columns
Seriously damaged by the Herulian invasion of 267, repaired 407-412
Three churches built at the site in Byzantine times, including Megali Panagia, the city's first cathedral

w: A bare hillside where, from as early as 507 BC, ordinary Athenians gathered to vote in the world's first popular assemblies - the literal birthplace of democracy, a few hundred metres from the Acropolis. No temple, no columns, just a retaining wall and a speaker's platform.
s: The bare hillside where democracy was invented
_facts: Hill in central Athens where Athenians hosted popular assemblies from as early as 507 BC
One of the earliest and most important sites in the creation of democracy
Located less than 1 km west of the Acropolis
Probable prototype for the Greek theatre auditorium

w: The potters' quarter that gave English the word 'ceramic', straddling the Dipylon Gate and the banks of the Eridanos - and also the site of ancient Athens's most important cemetery, its Sacred Way to Eleusis once lined with elaborate funerary sculpture.
s: The quarter that gave us the word 'ceramic'
_facts: Area of Athens northwest of the Acropolis, within and outside the ancient city walls
The potters' quarter, origin of the English word 'ceramic'
Site of an important ancient cemetery with funerary sculptures along the Sacred Way to Eleusis

w: A family mansion turned museum, endowed in 1930 by Antonis Benakis in memory of his father and now home to over 100,000 artefacts spanning the whole of Greek history. It once held Islamic art and Chinese porcelain too, before a 2000 reorganisation spun those off into satellite museums.
s: 100,000 artefacts inside a Benakis family mansion
_facts: Museum established and endowed in 1930 by Antonis Benakis, housed in the Benakis family mansion
Over 100,000 artefacts from Greek history
Originally also held Islamic art and Chinese porcelain; 2000 reopening spun those into satellite museums

w: The seat of the Archbishop of Athens and All Greece, known to locals simply as the Metropolis - the cathedral at the centre of Greek Orthodox religious life in the capital, its plain popular name saying more about its role than any architectural description could.
s: Seat of the Archbishop of All Greece
_facts: Cathedral church of the Archbishopric of Athens and all of Greece
Popularly known as the Metropolis or Mitropoli

w: A Roman-era mausoleum on Mouseion Hill honouring Gaius Julius Antiochus Epiphanes Philopappos, an exiled prince of the Kingdom of Commagene who died in Athens in AD 116. From the hilltop beside it comes one of the best skyline views in the city.
s: An exiled prince's tomb with Athens's best view
_facts: Ancient Roman mausoleum and monument dedicated to Gaius Julius Antiochus Epiphanes Philopappos (65-116 AD)
Philopappos was a prince from the Kingdom of Commagene
Located on Mouseion Hill, southwest of the Acropolis

w: A flea-market neighbourhood named for the 'little monastery' - the Church of the Pantanassa - that still stands on its namesake square. Pandrossou and Adrianou streets are lined with clothing boutiques, souvenirs and bargain-hunters' finds beneath the Acropolis.
_facts: Flea market neighbourhood in the old town of Athens, one of the main shopping districts
Named after Monastiraki Square, itself named for the Church of the Pantanassa
Main streets are Pandrossou Street and Adrianou Street

w: Fifteen and a half hectares of shade behind the Greek Parliament, laid out as the Royal Garden until 1974 and still scattered with ancient column drums, Corinthian capitals and mosaics unearthed on site. Busts of Kapodistrias and Solomos stand quietly among the paths.
s: A royal garden hiding ancient ruins underfoot
_facts: Public park of 15.5 hectares in central Athens, formerly the Royal Garden until 1974
Encloses ancient ruins, column drums, Corinthian capitals, and mosaics
Busts of Ioannis Kapodistrias, Jean-Gabriel Eynard, Dionysios Solomos, and Aristotelis Valaoritis

w: The Painted Portico, raised around 460 BC on the north side of the Agora and famous for the war-booty and battle paintings displayed inside. Zeno of Citium taught philosophy from its colonnade - and the school he founded took its name directly from this stoa: Stoicism.
s: The porch that gave philosophy the word 'Stoic'
_facts: Doric stoa erected around 460 BC on the north side of the Ancient Agora of Athens
Famous for paintings and war-booty displayed within it
Associated with ancient Greek philosophy, especially the origin of Stoicism
